es.summary: La resistencia a los antibióticos es la capacidad de las bacterias para sobrevivir y multiplicarse pese a la exposición a fármacos antimicrobianos.
key_points: Mecanismos: enzimas que inactivan, bombas de eflujo, alteración de sitios diana y reducción de permeabilidad.
Transferencia genética horizontal permite la diseminación rápida de genes de resistencia.
El uso inadecuado y la falta de adherencia al tratamiento son factores de riesgo principales.
El personal de enfermería debe promover la terapia adecuada y la vigilancia microbiológica.
La resistencia aumenta la morbilidad, la duración de la hospitalización y los costos de salud.

mechanism: Producción de enzimas (p. ej., beta‑lactamasas) que degradan el antibiótico.
Modificación del sitio de unión del fármaco, disminuyendo su afinidad.
Bombas de eflujo que expulsan el antibiótico fuera de la célula bacteriana.
Disminución de la permeabilidad de la membrana externa (por cambios en porinas).
Formación de biofilm que protege a la bacteria del agente antimicrobiano.
Transferencia de genes de resistencia mediante plasmidios, transposones o bacteriófagos.
nursing_care: Obtener cultivo y antibiograma antes de iniciar terapia empírica.
Monitorear signos de infección: fiebre, leucocitosis, dolor, secreción.
Evaluar respuesta clínica y laboratorial al antibiótico prescrito.
Retener la dosis si el paciente presenta reacción alérgica o toxicidad evidente.
Aplicar precauciones de aislamiento según el organismo resistente identificado.
Reportar al médico y al comité de control de infecciones cualquier aislamiento de microorganismo resistente.
patient_teaching: Completar el ciclo completo del antibiótico aunque mejore el cuadro.
No compartir antibióticos ni usar restos de tratamientos anteriores.
Informar al profesional si se olvida una dosis o aparecen efectos adversos.
Practicar higiene de manos y medidas de prevención de infecciones.
Entender la importancia de la vacunación para reducir la necesidad de antibióticos.

outcomes: Control de la infección: ausencia de signos de infección en 48‑72 h
Adherencia al tratamiento: 100 % de cumplimiento del régimen antibiótico prescrito

interventions.action: Obtener y documentar cultivo y antibiograma antes de iniciar antibiótico
interventions.rationale: Permite seleccionar terapia dirigida y evitar uso innecesario de antibióticos de amplio espectro

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre la importancia de completar el ciclo del antibiótico
interventions.rationale: Reduce la probabilidad de supervivencia de bacterias parcialmente expuestas

interventions.action: Monitorear temperatura, recuento de leucocitos y signos locales de infección cada 4 h
interventions.rationale: Detecta tempranamente fracaso terapéutico o complicaciones

interventions.action: Aplicar aislamiento de contacto o precauciones según protocolo institucional
interventions.rationale: Previene la transmisión de organismos resistentes a otros pacientes

interventions.action: Revisar historial de alergias y reacciones previas a antibióticos antes de la administración
interventions.rationale: Evita reacciones adversas que podrían interrumpir la terapia

en.summary: Antibiotic resistance is the ability of bacteria to survive and multiply despite exposure to antimicrobial drugs.
key_points: Mechanisms: enzymes that inactivate, efflux pumps, alteration of target sites, and reduced permeability.
Horizontal genetic transfer allows rapid dissemination of resistance genes.
Inappropriate use and lack of adherence to treatment are major risk factors.
Nursing staff must promote appropriate therapy and microbiologic surveillance.
Resistance increases morbidity, length of hospitalization, and health care costs.

mechanism: Production of enzymes (e.g., beta‑lactamases) that degrade the antibiotic.
Modification of the drug binding site, decreasing its affinity.
Efflux pumps that expel the antibiotic from the bacterial cell.
Reduced permeability of the outer membrane (due to porin changes).
Biofilm formation that protects the bacteria from the antimicrobial agent.
Transfer of resistance genes via plasmids, transposons, or bacteriophages.
nursing_care: Obtain culture and antibiogram before starting empirical therapy.
Monitor signs of infection: fever, leukocytosis, pain, discharge.
Assess clinical and laboratory response to the prescribed antibiotic.
Hold the dose if the patient shows allergic reaction or evident toxicity.
Apply isolation precautions according to the identified resistant organism.
Report to the physician and infection control committee any isolation of a resistant microorganism.
patient_teaching: Complete the full antibiotic course even if symptoms improve.
Do not share antibiotics or use leftovers from previous treatments.
Inform the professional if a dose is missed or adverse effects appear.
Practice hand hygiene and infection prevention measures.
Understand the importance of vaccination to reduce the need for antibiotics.

outcomes: Infection control: absence of infection signs within 48‑72 h
Treatment adherence: 100 % compliance with prescribed antibiotic regimen

interventions.action: Obtain and document culture and antibiogram before starting antibiotic
interventions.rationale: Allows selection of targeted therapy and avoids unnecessary use of broad‑spectrum antibiotics

interventions.action: Educate the patient on the importance of completing the antibiotic course
interventions.rationale: Reduces the likelihood of survival of partially exposed bacteria

interventions.action: Monitor temperature, white blood cell count, and local infection signs every 4 h
interventions.rationale: Detects early therapeutic failure or complications

interventions.action: Apply contact isolation or precautions per institutional protocol
interventions.rationale: Prevents transmission of resistant organisms to other patients

interventions.action: Review allergy history and prior antibiotic reactions before administration
interventions.rationale: Avoids adverse reactions that could interrupt therapy

summary.0.quote: Antibiotic drug resistance is the process by which bacteria become less responsive to antibiotics over time.

key_points.0.quote: These changes can include modification of antibiotic targets (e.g., bacterial DNA or proteins) or the ability to remove a drug from the bacterial cell more effectively.

key_points.3.quote: One of the most important roles of the nurse in preventing antibiotic resistance is educating patients about taking their antibiotics as prescribed (National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, 2020).

sections.mechanism.0.quote: Beta-lactamase is one such enzyme; it is produced in resistant bacteria to cleave the beta-lactam ring found in drugs like penicillin to render it ineffective.

sections.mechanism.1.quote: These changes can include modification of antibiotic targets (e.g., bacterial DNA or proteins) or the ability to remove a drug from the bacterial cell more effectively.

sections.mechanism.2.quote: Others use pumps within their cell wall to remove the antibiotics after they enter the cell.

sections.mechanism.3.quote: Some bacteria have outer membranes that antibiotics cannot penetrate.

sections.nursing_care.4.quote: Isolation protocols: Use isolation techniques for patients with resistant infections to prevent transmission to others.

sections.patient_teaching.0.quote: For this reason, nurses must emphasize the importance of finishing the entire course of antibiotics, even if the patient reports improved symptoms, and not sharing medications with others.

sections.patient_teaching.3.quote: Enhance infection control practices, including hand hygiene and environmental cleaning, to prevent the spread of resistant bacteria.
